summary: A Stack Overflow question asking for existing practical tools or methods to compress correlated floating-point time-series data, ideally beating gzip while staying comparable in speed, with a controlled, bounded precision reduction acceptable. The page includes several answers: XOR-based differencing with mantissa/exponent splitting, truncating low-order mantissa bits (with a C and Python example), HDF5-style byte shuffling and float16 conversion, the zfp, TurboTranspose/TurboPFor and icapp tools, and a zstd tar command. Navigation and site boilerplate are ignored.
one_line: Stack Overflow question and answers on lossless and controlled-precision compression of correlated floating-point time-series data, compared against gzip.
key_facts: The question was asked on Dec 25, 2011 and last modified about 1 year, 2 months before the snapshot, with 37k views.
The asker works with large data files that are series of correlated doubles describing a function of time.
The asker wants a controlled way to bound how many digits are kept, and says a tool comparable to gzip in speed would be excellent.
The asker says they are looking for existing practical tools rather than a paper describing how to implement something.
One answer notes that 1.2345 is stored as 0x3ff3c083126e978d in binary double precision.
Zeroing the least significant 24 bits of 1.2345 gives 0x3ff3c08312000000, still accurate to about 9 decimal digits, with a difference of 1.6e-9.
For single-precision floats there are 23 fraction bits, of which up to 22 can be zeroed; for double precision there are 52, of which up to 51 can be zeroed.
One answer recommends the HDF5 technique of shuffling, which groups each byte of N floating point values together.
Another answer reports that converting data to float16 and back to float32 can shrink gzipped file sizes by around 40-60 per cent.
That answer notes the maximum float16 value is 65504, so data may need scaling first, and reports a maximum fractional difference of about 0.00048.
An answer recommends the zfp tool as an existing option for compressing floating-point data.
A later answer lists the TurboTranspose, TurboPFor and icapp tools and says icapp can test these methods on linux and windows.
A zstd-based answer gives tar commands using --use-compress-program=zstd to compress, decompress and list archives.
